summary: Defines an IPv6 provider-based unicast address format, where addresses are tied to the provider that hands them out. It was replaced by RFC 2374.

plainLanguage.summary: Addresses are organized so that the company supplying your internet is part of your address.

questions: what is ipv6 provider based addressing
how does ipv6 address allocation hierarchy work
subtitle: IPv6 addresses that embed your Internet provider's identity.

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses need a hierarchical structure that allows efficient routing and address allocation across the global Internet.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses include a Registry ID (identifying the region), Provider ID (identifying your ISP), and Subscriber ID (identifying you), with 64 bits left for the subscriber to organize locally.
tldr.outcome: This format enabled scalable Internet routing by allowing routers to aggregate addresses by provider and region, though it was later obsoleted by RFC 2374 which offered more flexibility.

today: RFC 2374 obsoleted this address format, which was a Proposed Standard when first issued.

sections.title: Introduction to IPv6 Provider-Based Addresses
sections.content:
This RFC defines how to structure IPv6 addresses so that they reflect the hierarchy of Internet service providers and regional registries. IPv6 is the next generation Internet Protocol, using 128-bit addresses instead of IPv4's 32-bit addresses. The provider-based format makes it possible for routers to find shorter, more efficient routing rules by aggregating addresses by provider.

The address format was designed to work with distributed address allocation, where regional registries (like RIPE NCC in Europe and APNIC in Asia) hand out blocks to providers, who then hand out blocks to customers.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a way to organize really long addresses so that they tell a story: what region you are in, what company gives you Internet, and who you are at that company.

sections.title: The Address Structure
sections.content:
A provider-based IPv6 address is divided into five parts. The first 3 bits are always 010, marking it as this type of address. Next come 5 bits for the Registry ID (identifying which of the four regional registries allocated the address). Then comes a variable-length Provider ID (unique within the registry), then the Subscriber ID (unique within the provider), and finally 64 bits for the local part that the subscriber can organize however they want.

The address format is: 010 | RegistryID (5 bits) | ProviderID (n bits) | SubscriberID (56-n bits) | Intra-Subscriber (64 bits). Each registry can decide how many bits to give to providers and how many to keep for subscribers.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is like a postal address. The first part says which big region, the next part says which company, the next part says which customer of that company, and the last part is up to the customer to use however they like.

sections.title: Registry and Provider Allocation
sections.content:
The RFC defines four Registry IDs in binary: 10000 for Multi-Regional (IANA), 01000 for RIPE NCC, 11000 for INTERNIC, and 00100 for APNIC. These match the four organizations that were managing IP address allocation at the time.

Within each registry, providers get their own Provider IDs. A registry can also create an intermediate layer by having National Registries allocate to providers within each country. The RFC leaves the details of how to split the remaining bits to each registry, to give flexibility for different numbers of providers and different growth patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of the world have different address managers. Each one gets a code, and each of them decides how to split up the addresses among the Internet companies in their region.

sections.title: Subscriber and Local Address Space
sections.content:
The Subscriber ID part is left to the provider to organize. Providers may group subscribers by region (Subscriber-Region ID) to control traffic flow when they are connected to other providers at multiple points.

The 64-bit local part (Intra-Subscriber) is entirely up to the subscriber. The RFC recommends using IPv6 stateless auto-configuration with 48-bit MAC addresses as Interface IDs, leaving 16 bits for subnet IDs. This allows subscribers to have up to 65,535 subnets, which the authors thought would be enough for all but the largest organizations. Very large subscribers can ask their provider for multiple Subscriber ID blocks or even their own Provider ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Your company gives you a big block of addresses and says 'do whatever you want with this.' You can split it into departments, buildings, or anything else.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 2374 replaced this address format in 1998 with a more flexible scheme that does not embed as much hierarchy into the address itself. However, provider-based addressing influenced how IPv6 address allocation actually works in practice, and understanding this format is helpful for understanding modern IPv6 address space management.
sections.plainLanguage: This way of organizing addresses was replaced by a simpler method, but the ideas behind it still influence how Internet companies hand out addresses today.
